The next verse exposes the same people as tyrannical in force, extending the critique of their monumental self-assertion.
Hud's repeated call to fear God and obey him provides the corrective response to the building-for-permanence impulse.
The warning recalls that their material capacity is supplied by God, not self-secured through their works.
Cattle and sons name the resources underlying the prosperous, enduring settlement imagined in the focus.
Gardens and springs complete the account of the settled abundance that makes their permanence-seeking construction intelligible.
Hud frames that prosperity and conduct against fear of a tremendous day's punishment.
Their indifference to warning clarifies the resistance surrounding the critique of their monuments.
Their appeal to ancestral custom helps explain how their self-assertive practice is normalized.
Their denial of punishment states the confidence that accompanies their imagined security.
Their destruction decisively contradicts their expectation of remaining forever.
The passage's closing sign and rejection formula frames the focus within the Ad narrative's warning.
Hud is sent to Ad with a call to worship God, supplying the wider prophetic setting for the focus passage.
The reminder that Ad succeeded earlier peoples and were increased in stature qualifies their confidence in strength and settlement.
The announced wrath and waiting contest counter the people's apparent confidence in their enduring position.
Ad's destruction shows that their collective power and habitation did not secure permanence.
Hud's address to his people, Ad, and call to worship God gives the fuller narrative frame for 26:129.
Hud links turning to God with rain and added strength, distinguishing granted strength from self-exalting durability.
Hud's deliverance and Ad's destruction establish the actual outcome of the people criticized in the focus.
Ad's curse in this world and the next directly overturns any claim to an enduring legacy.
The brother of Ad warns his people amid the sand dunes, locating their threat within a concrete settled landscape.
The cloud they expected as rain becomes the destructive punishment they were promised, reversing their confidence in material provision.
The wind destroys everything by God's command, showing the fragility of Ad's apparently durable world.
Ad's boast that none is stronger than them names the pride that also animates their monumental construction.
A humiliating wind exposes the failure of Ad's asserted strength and lasting security.
Iram, characterized by its lofty pillars, is a close architectural and civilizational parallel to the focus's construction imagery.
Its unmatched built achievement sharpens the contrast between exceptional construction and impermanence.
Thamud's carving of homes from rock closely parallels the focus's theme of durable habitation made by human craft.
Ad's rejection initiates the destruction narrative that answers their presumption of enduring power.
The relentless wind gives the physical means by which Ad's apparent permanence is undone.
The violent wind sent against Ad provides another direct counterpoint to their confidence in lasting strength.
Their bodies left like hollow palm trunks makes the collapse of their collective permanence vivid.
The question whether any remnant remains gives the final negation of Ad's aspiration to endure.
